questions.q: What does the sys.databases catalog view provide?
options: One row per database on the instance, with columns covering most built-in configuration like recovery model and state
One row per table across every database
A list of only offline databases
Custom metadata attached with sp_addextendedproperty
questions.explain: sys.databases exposes one row per database with columns like recovery_model_desc, compatibility_level, state_desc, and is_read_only — the first place to audit configuration across an instance.

questions.q: When is DATABASEPROPERTYEX() the more natural choice over sys.databases?
options: When you need one specific property for one specific database, often inside a script or conditional check
When you need every property for every database at once
When you need to change a property, not just read it
It is never a better choice than sys.databases
questions.explain: DATABASEPROPERTYEX() returns a single named property for a single named database — convenient for a targeted check inside a script.

options: It lets you attach custom name/value metadata (like database ownership or data classification) that SQL Server has no built-in column for
It changes the database's recovery model
It creates a new filegroup
It is used only to rename a database
questions.explain: sp_addextendedproperty attaches arbitrary metadata to a database or any object inside it — useful for things SQL Server doesn't natively track, like which team owns a database.

questions.q: How do you query metadata that was added with sp_addextendedproperty?
options: Via the sys.extended_properties catalog view or the fn_listextendedproperty function
Via sys.databases only
Via DBCC CHECKDB
Extended properties cannot be queried back once set
questions.explain: sys.extended_properties and fn_listextendedproperty are the two ways to read back custom metadata attached with sp_addextendedproperty.

questions.q: When calling sp_addextendedproperty with no @level0type or @level1type arguments, where does the property attach?
options: At the database level itself
To every table in the database simultaneously
To the transaction log file only
It causes an error and requires those arguments
questions.explain: Omitting the level0/level1 type arguments attaches the extended property to the database itself, rather than to a specific object inside it.
